name: Laser hair-growth helmet/cap

lead: Laser caps and helmets are worn at home with the aim of slowing hair loss and getting thicker, denser hair on the scalp. People use them for androgenetic alopecia, the common pattern thinning.

Low-power red laser light is thought to act on follicle cells to stimulate them. A 2012 review found little evidence, 2015 and 2017 reviews reported tentative benefit (10 of 11 trials in the 2017 review showed improvement), and reviewers have asked for larger long-term double-blind trials.

paras: Users wear the cap or helmet for short sessions several times a week, often alongside other hair-loss routines, and results are judged over months. Several devices are FDA-cleared, and prices vary widely, with premium helmets costing around $2,000 according to one forum user.
Reported side effects are mild pain or skin irritation. Long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown, and some devices call for eye protection during use.

angle.text: Users wear laser caps and helmets at home hoping to slow hair loss and thicken hair in androgenetic alopecia. Low-level laser light is meant to stimulate follicles, and reviews have reported mixed-to-tentative benefit while asking for larger trials.

lead: Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices that apply low-level laser or light therapy (LLLT, also called photobiomodulation) to the scalp. People use them at home, typically for a set number of minutes on a regular schedule, with the aim of thickening hair and slowing or reversing androgenetic alopecia, so the scalp looks denser. Wikipedia lists hats, combs and helmets among home-use LLLT options [1].

Reviews of laser therapy for hair loss span mixed to positive: a 2012 review found little support, 2014 reviews were mixed, and 2015 and 2017 reviews reported tentative benefit, with 10 of 11 trials in the 2017 review showing significant improvement versus baseline or controls [1]. Wikipedia reports that LLLT has been shown to increase hair density in both men and women, that device format and treatment duration did not appear to change effectiveness, and that some reviews suggest it may work as well as or better than minoxidil and finasteride, with larger long-term double-blind trials called for [1].

A 16-week sham-controlled trial of a helmet-type device in 60 Korean participants with androgenetic alopecia reported hair density gains of about 42 hairs per square centimetre in the device group versus under 1 in the sham group [2]. On looksmax.org, users describe pairing a laser helmet with finasteride and other measures [3].
infobox: Up to about $2,000 for some helmets (forum report) [3]

paras: The main proposed mechanism involves the mitochondrial enzyme cytochrome c oxidase, and effects appear limited to certain wavelengths; red and infrared light appear more effective for androgenetic alopecia, according to Wikipedia. Effectiveness is still under investigation [1].
Hungarian physician Endre Mester reported in 1967 that hair regrew faster in mice treated with a low-power laser, an observation made when a faulty laser was used in an experiment [1].

A 2017 review reported 10 of 11 trials showing significant improvement in androgenetic alopecia versus baseline or controls. Reviews describe device type and treatment duration as not changing effectiveness, and one meta-analysis gave lasers more weight than LEDs [1].

A 2020 randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial in Medicine tested a helmet-type device for 16 weeks in 60 participants at two Korean institutions. Hair density rose by 41.90 hairs/cm2 in the device group versus 0.72 in the sham group, and hair thickness rose by 7.50 micrometres versus a fall of 15.03 in the sham group. Satisfaction scores were slightly higher in the device group without a statistically significant difference. The manufacturer funded the study, and the authors cite short follow-up, small sample and possible measurement bias as limitations [2].

Reported side effects include mild pain or skin irritation; long-term effects are unknown and some devices require eye protection [1]. The 2020 helmet trial recorded no adverse events over 16 weeks, and earlier trials it cites reported mild effects such as headache, dry skin, itching and redness [2].
On looksmax.org, users describe combining a laser helmet with finasteride and other measures, with one poster describing a premium helmet costing about $2,000 used for about 12 minutes a day [3].

Reviews and sham-controlled trials of low-level light devices for androgenetic alopecia are summarised above [1][2]. Larger, long-term, double-blind trials are called for, and most evidence comes from short trials, some funded by device makers [1][2].
